name: How do you price an open-floor-plan conversion for a house with hidden damage?

mainEntity.name: How should you budget for an open-floor-plan conversion when hidden damage may be found after demolition?
mainEntity.text: How should you budget for an open-floor-plan conversion when hidden damage may be found after demolition?

acceptedAnswer.text: Hidden damage is common in remodels, especially in older homes. Once the wall is opened, contractors may find dry rot, previous patchwork framing, termite damage, undersized wiring, or unpermitted changes that must be corrected before the opening can be finished. That is why open-floor-plan budgets should include a contingency rather than only the base estimate. A practical approach is to reserve extra funds for structural repairs and finish surprises so the project does not stall halfway through demolition. Homeowners should also ask the contractor how change orders are handled and how quickly unexpected conditions are documented. The best budget is one that assumes the house will reveal something once construction starts, because that is often exactly what happens.
acceptedAnswer.description: Budget extra contingency because hidden issues like dry rot, termite damage, outdated wiring, or foundation concerns can appear once the wall is opened. A contingency reserve helps keep the project moving.
